output:
*Interview with Dr Casimir Vauthier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Docteur, thank you for waiting. I know the hour and the cold. You have known the Monnier family a long time, I think.

DR VAUTHIER: Thirty years, Inspector, very nearly. I attended the children when there were children, and I have sat at this table more often than at my own. Aurèle was my friend. I am still trying to take that in.

MATTHEY: Then you know the house. What was Monsieur Monnier to you, and what was he to his wife?

DR VAUTHIER: To me he was the best company in the town on a bad evening and the worst on a good one. He could not leave a piece of work alone, and he could not leave a man alone either. As for Odile, I will leave that to Odile. Thirty years of marriage wear two people smooth. I think they were smooth with each other, and comfortable with it.

MATTHEY: You attended his brother Jules in 1889.

DR VAUTHIER: I did. It was a long illness and I was with him at the end. Aurèle sat with his brother through it, and I remember him quiet in that room, which was rare.

MATTHEY: You have examined Monsieur Monnier tonight.

DR VAUTHIER: I have. You will have the details from the police surgeon, but I can tell you what I saw. A blow to the back of the head, from behind, by something heavy with a hard face. Death would have been very quick. He would not have known much about it.

MATTHEY: Let us come to the evening. Tell me about dinner.

DR VAUTHIER: Aurèle gave us dinner, as he does every year on the last night of the century. When the temple bell struck nine, he made each of us bring out our watch, and he told each owner what was wrong with it. I am a physician, Inspector. I do not carry a watch for the look of it. Mine was two minutes ahead of the bell. He had his remark about that, and I will not repeat it.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

DR VAUTHIER: Madame and I played piquet in the salon. We play most evenings, when she allows me to win. We played until a quarter to eleven by my watch, when I went out to the hall to fetch my cigar case from my coat. I had forgotten it. Madame began to play the piano as I went out, and she stopped when I came back.

MATTHEY: Which piece did she play?

DR VAUTHIER: Chopin. She plays Chopin when something is on her mind, and she does not care to be asked about it. I did not ask.

MATTHEY: You came back and sat down again. What happened then?

DR VAUTHIER: The hall clock struck eleven a moment after I sat down again. It strikes by its own face. Aurèle was fond of it for that.

MATTHEY: You know the regulator upstairs.

DR VAUTHIER: I do. He once told me it was the only honest clock in Neuchâtel. I understand it had stopped when they found him. A regulator stops with its master, Inspector. That is the sentiment of the thing, and I will not pretend it is anything more.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Docteur. Is there anything you wish to add?

DR VAUTHIER: Only this. *Festina lente*, the old men said, and Aurèle lived by it, though he never admitted to it. Whoever did this was not in a hurry, and I do not think it was a stranger's hand.

MATTHEY: Thank you. That will be all for now.
